Dielectric function in WSe2 monolayer Wigner crystal

Tiberius O. Cheche Affiliation: Department of Physics, National Cheng-Kung University, Tainan, Taiwan 704    Yia-Chung Chang* Affiliation: Department of Physics, National Cheng-Kung University, Tainan, Taiwan 704 Affiliation: Research Center for Applied Sciences, Academia Sinica, Taipei, Taiwan 11529
*Email: yiachang@gate.sinica.edu.tw
Abstract

We develop a Hartree-Fock numerical method for computing the band structure of a two-dimensional Wigner crystal in an electron gas at zero temperature. The ground state is assumed to be fully spin-polarized. Single-particle excitation spectra are evaluated in spin-conserving channel. As an application, we use the developed code to compute the static dielectric function ϵ\epsilon(q,0) of a Wigner-crystal state formed in a two-dimensional transition-metal dichalcogenide, specifically monolayer WSe2. The dielectric response is obtained from the Hartree-Fock band structure and eigenfunctions through a static Lindhard-type polarizability. The method provides a theoretical tool for investigating screening, band-structure reconstruction, and interaction effects in low-density two-dimensional systems, with possible relevance for future experimental studies.

1 Introduction

The possibility of electron crystallization was first proposed by Wigner in his seminal studies of the interacting electron gas [21, 22]. In the low-density regime, the Coulomb interaction energy dominates over the kinetic energy, and the electron gas can lower its total energy by forming a spatially ordered crystalline state, now known as the Wigner-crystal. Subsequent theoretical work established the basic static and dynamical properties of such ordered electron states. In particular, Bonsall and Maradudin analyzed the classical two-dimensional (2D) Wigner-crystal, showing that the triangular lattice has the lowest energy among the 2D Bravais lattices, and computed its phonon spectrum and long-wavelength dielectric response [4].

More quantitative quantum descriptions of Wigner crystallization have been developed within both many-body and mean-field frameworks. Hartree–Fock approaches have been used to construct broken-symmetry crystalline solutions, to analyze spin polarization and excitation channels, and to compute the electronic structure of Wigner-crystal states [19, 3, 8]. Quantum Monte Carlo calculations have provided accurate benchmarks for the ground-state energy and for the liquid–crystal phase boundary in two- and three-dimensional electron gases [17, 7].

Recent experimental advances in atomically thin semiconductors have provided direct motivation for applying Wigner-crystal theory to 2D transition-metal dichalcogenide (TMD) materials. Zhou et al. reported bilayer Wigner crystals in MoSe2 heterostructures separated by hexagonal boron nitride, without requiring an external magnetic field or a moiré potential, and investigated their quantum and thermal melting behavior [27]. Smoleński et al. observed signatures of an electronic Wigner crystal in a pristine monolayer semiconductor at low carrier density, emphasizing the role of large effective mass and reduced dielectric screening in stabilizing zero-field crystallization [14]. More recently, Zhang et al. used exciton spectroscopy in monolayer WSe2 to probe Wigner polarons and to distinguish static Umklapp signatures from dynamic polaron resonances [24]. In a related moiré setting, Tang et al. studied bandwidth-controlled metal–insulator transitions in a MoSe2/WS2 superlattice and highlighted dielectric response as a probe of interaction-driven Wigner–Mott physics [18].

A 2D Wigner crystal is characterized by a spatially modulated charge density with the periodicity of a triangular lattice. In the present work, we adopt a self-consistent Hartree–Fock approach to compute the single-particle band structure of such a crystalline state and its static dielectric response. The calculation is performed within a restricted Hartree–Fock framework, in which the single-particle orbitals and the charge density are not constrained to preserve the continuous translational symmetry of the uniform electron gas. The self-consistent solution is therefore allowed to develop crystalline density harmonics. In the present implementation, the ground state is assumed to be fully spin-polarized. Consequently, exchange acts only between states with the same spin projection, whereas the opposite-spin particle channel is described by the Hartree contribution evaluated in the frozen Hartree potential generated by the converged spin-polarized Hartree–Fock Wigner-crystal density.

The manuscript is organized as follows. Theory section introduces the Hartree–Fock formulation of the spin-polarized Wigner crystal, its expansion in the plane-wave basis |𝐤+𝐆⟩\left\lvert\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}\right\rangle, and the Lindhard-type expression used to compute the static dielectric response of the insulating crystalline state. Numerical code and results section describes the numerical implementation and presents the calculated band structures and dielectric functions. Conclusions section summarizes the main conclusions. Additional technical details are provided in Supporting Information.

2 Theory

2.1 Hartree–Fock equation in the 𝐤+𝐆\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G} basis

The self-consistent Wigner-crystal state is periodic with respect to the emergent triangular lattice. The Hartree–Fock (HF) orbitals can therefore be expanded in Bloch form as

ψn​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)=1A​∑𝐆Zn​𝐆​σ​(𝐤)​ei⁡(𝐤+𝐆)⋅𝐫,\psi_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{A}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}}Z_{n\mathbf{G}\sigma}(\mathbf{k})e^{i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}}, (1)

where AA is the normalization area, σ\sigma is the spin projection, 𝐤\mathbf{k} belongs to the first Brillouin zone of the Wigner-crystal lattice, and 𝐆\mathbf{G} are reciprocal-lattice vectors. Projection onto the plane-wave basis A−1/2ei⁡(𝐤+𝐆)⋅𝐫A^{-1/2}e^{i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}} gives the matrix eigenvalue problem

∑𝐆′h𝐆𝐆′σ​(𝐤)​Zn​𝐆′​σ​(𝐤)=εn​𝐤​σ​Zn​𝐆​σ​(𝐤),\sum_{\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}h_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}^{\sigma}(\mathbf{k})Z_{n\mathbf{G}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{k})=\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}Z_{n\mathbf{G}\sigma}(\mathbf{k}), (2)

with

h𝐆𝐆′σ​(𝐤)=T𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤)+V𝐆𝐆′H−Σ𝐆𝐆′F,σ​(𝐤).h_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}^{\sigma}(\mathbf{k})=T_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})+V^{H}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}-\Sigma^{F,\sigma}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}). (3)

For a parabolic effective-mass band and in the absence of an external potential, the kinetic contribution is diagonal,

T𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤)=ℏ2​|𝐤+𝐆|22​m∗​δ𝐆𝐆′,T_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})=\frac{\hbar^{2}|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}|^{2}}{2m^{*}}\delta_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}, (4)

where m∗m^{*} is the electron effective mass in the 2D material. The Hartree term is local and independent of 𝐤\mathbf{k}. In reciprocal space,

V𝐆𝐆′H=VH​(𝐆−𝐆′)=v~​(𝐆−𝐆′)​n~​(𝐆−𝐆′),V^{H}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}=V_{H}(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}^{\prime})=\widetilde{v}(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}^{\prime})\,\widetilde{n}(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}^{\prime}), (5)

where v~​(𝐐)\widetilde{v}(\mathbf{Q}) is the Fourier transform of the interaction potential and n~​(𝐐)\widetilde{n}(\mathbf{Q}) is the self-consistent density Fourier coefficient.

The Fock term is nonlocal and spin diagonal. In the 𝐤+𝐆\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G} representation it is

Σ𝐆𝐆′F,σ​(𝐤)=∑ν′∈occ∑𝐤′w𝐤′​∑𝐆1Zν′​𝐆1​σ​(𝐤′)​Zν′,𝐆1−𝐆+𝐆′,σ∗​(𝐤′)​v~​[(𝐤+𝐆)−(𝐤′+𝐆1)],\Sigma^{F,\sigma}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})=\sum_{\nu^{\prime}\in\mathrm{occ}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}w_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}_{1}}Z_{\nu^{\prime}\mathbf{G}_{1}\sigma}(\mathbf{k}^{\prime})Z^{*}_{\nu^{\prime},\mathbf{G}_{1}-\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime},\sigma}(\mathbf{k}^{\prime})\,\widetilde{v}\!\left[(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})-(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}+\mathbf{G}_{1})\right], (6)

where w𝐤′w_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}} are the Brillouin-zone integration weights and ν′\nu^{\prime} labels the occupied HF bands entering the spin-resolved density matrix. Terms for which the shifted vector 𝐆1−𝐆+𝐆′\mathbf{G}_{1}-\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime} lies outside the retained plane-wave basis are omitted. In the fully spin-polarized one-band calculation considered here, only one spin sector is occupied and the occupied-band sum reduces to ν′=1\nu^{\prime}=1; consequently, exchange contributes only to the same-spin particle channel. The coordinate-space HF equation and the derivation of the matrix elements, including the reciprocal-lattice selection rule implicit in Eq. (6), are given in SI.1.

For the band-structure calculations reported below, the target momenta 𝐤\mathbf{k} are taken in the irreducible Γ\Gamma–KK–MM wedge, while the source sum over 𝐤′\mathbf{k}^{\prime} in Eq. (6) is evaluated explicitly over the full Brillouin-zone mesh reconstructed from the wedge solution. Thus the exchange field is built from the full Brillouin zone rather than from a symmetry-reduced source sum. The coefficients Zn​𝐆​σ​(𝐤)Z_{n\mathbf{G}\sigma}(\mathbf{k}) are obtained self-consistently: at a given iteration, the density harmonics ηW​(𝐐)\eta_{W}(\mathbf{Q}) define the Hartree contribution, whereas the occupied eigenvectors from the previous iteration define the Fock contribution.

The effective electrostatic interaction between charge carriers confined to a 2D semiconductor can be described by the Keldysh interaction [9, 11, 5]. In reciprocal space, for an isotropic dielectric environment, we write

v~K​(q)=2​π​e2ε​q​(1+q​ρ0).\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{K}}(q)=\frac{2\pi e^{2}}{\varepsilon q\left(1+q\rho_{0}\right)}. (7)

Here, qq denotes the wave-vector length, ε\varepsilon is the effective dielectric constant of the medium surrounding the monolayer, and ρ0\rho_{0} is the Keldysh screening length. In the convention used here, ρ0=κ/(2​ε)\rho_{0}=\kappa/(2\varepsilon), where κ\kappa denotes the in-plane polarizability of the 2D material.

After diagonalizing Eq. (2) for all 𝐤\mathbf{k} points, the new eigenvectors are used to reconstruct the density harmonics according to

ηW​(𝐐)=1AW​∑ν∈occ∑𝐤w𝐤​∑𝐆Zν​𝐆​σ∗​(𝐤)​Zν,𝐆+𝐐,σ​(𝐤),\eta_{W}(\mathbf{Q})=\frac{1}{A_{W}}\sum_{\nu\in\mathrm{occ}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}}Z^{*}_{\nu\mathbf{G}\sigma}(\mathbf{k})Z_{\nu,\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{Q},\sigma}(\mathbf{k}), (8)

where AWA_{W} is the Wigner-crystal primitive-cell area and the Brillouin-zone weights are normalized as ∑𝐤w𝐤=1\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}=1. The index ν\nu is a dummy occupied-band index used in the density reconstruction. In the present one-band spin-polarized implementation, the sum over occupied bands contains only the lowest occupied band and as mentioned ν=1\nu=1. The numerical implementation uses an irreducible wedge of the Brillouin zone, but the density reconstruction is equivalent to a full-zone summation after applying the symmetry images of the eigenvectors. The self-consistency loop is therefore closed by repeatedly updating the pair {Zn​𝐆​σ​(𝐤),ηW​(𝐐)}\{Z_{n\mathbf{G}\sigma}(\mathbf{k}),\eta_{W}(\mathbf{Q})\} until convergence.

The self-consistent Hartree–Fock cycle is initialized from a periodic charge density with the periodicity of the Wigner-crystal lattice. Since the density is periodic over the Wigner-Seitz cell of area AWA_{W}, it can be expanded in reciprocal-lattice harmonics,

n(0)​(𝐫)=∑𝐐ηW(0)​(𝐐)​ei​𝐐⋅𝐫,n^{(0)}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{Q}}\eta_{W}^{(0)}(\mathbf{Q})e^{i\mathbf{Q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}, (9)

where 𝐐=m​𝐛1+n​𝐛2\mathbf{Q}=m\mathbf{b}_{1}+n\mathbf{b}_{2}, with m,n∈ℤm,n\in\mathbb{Z}, denotes a reciprocal-lattice vector. For one electron per primitive cell, the normalization condition is ηW(0)​(𝟎)=1/AW\eta_{W}^{(0)}(\mathbf{0})=1/A_{W}.

For the initial state, we use localized Gaussian-like Bloch amplitudes in the plane-wave basis |𝐤+𝐆⟩\left\lvert\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}\right\rangle. For each wave vector 𝐤\mathbf{k} in the Brillouin-zone and 𝐆\mathbf{G} reciprocal lattice vector, the initial coefficients are taken as

F𝐤(0)​(𝐆)=exp[−|𝐤+𝐆|2/(2β)][∑𝐆′exp[−|𝐤+𝐆′|2/β]]1/2,F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{G})=\frac{\exp\left[-\left|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}\right|^{2}/(2\beta)\right]}{\left[\sum_{\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}\exp\left[-\left|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}\right|^{2}/\beta\right]\right]^{1/2}}, (10)

where β\beta controls the width of the initial packet in reciprocal space. In the numerical implementation, the input parameter is the dimensionless Gaussian width β0=β​(aB∗)2\beta_{0}=\beta(a_{B}^{*})^{2}, or equivalently β=β0/(aB∗)2\beta=\beta_{0}/(a_{B}^{*})^{2}, where β\beta is measured in nm-2. The effective Bohr radius is defined as aB∗=(ε​m0/m∗)​a0a_{B}^{*}=(\varepsilon m_{0}/m^{*})a_{0}, with a0a_{0} the Bohr radius in vacuum, m0m_{0} the free-electron mass, and ε\varepsilon the effective dielectric constant of the medium surrounding the monolayer.

The corresponding initial density harmonics are computed from the plane-wave coefficients as

ηW(0)​(𝐐)=1AW​∑𝐤w𝐤​∑𝐆F𝐤(0)​(𝐆)​F𝐤(0)​(𝐆+𝐐),\eta_{W}^{(0)}(\mathbf{Q})=\frac{1}{A_{W}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}}F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{G})F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{Q}), (11)

where the weights satisfy ∑𝐤w𝐤=1\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}=1. For a uniform full-BZ mesh, w𝐤=1/Nkw_{\mathbf{k}}=1/N_{k}, and Eq. (11) reduces to the explicit form with the prefactor 1/(AW​Nk)1/(A_{W}N_{k}). This construction guarantees the correct normalization condition, while providing a periodic crystalline initial guess for the subsequent self-consistent Hartree–Fock iterations. Proof of eqs. (8) and (11) is provided in SI.2.

2.2 Static dielectric function

The dielectric response of a Wigner-crystal can be discussed from complementary viewpoints. In the classical long-wavelength limit, the response is governed by the collective elastic and phonon modes of the electron lattice, as in the analysis of Bonsall and Maradudin for the 2D Wigner-crystal [4]. Screening and capacitive response have also been used experimentally as probes of Wigner-crystal melting and dynamics in high-mobility two-dimensional electron systems [6, 26]. The present calculation addresses a different, microscopic contribution: the static density response obtained from the self-consistent Hartree–Fock quasiparticle bands and eigenvectors of the crystalline state.

The formula used below is the insulating, folded-Brillouin-zone analogue of the independent-particle polarizability underlying the Lindhard response of the electron gas [10] and the Stern polarizability of the homogeneous two-dimensional electron gas [16]. Because the Wigner crystal is a periodic broken-symmetry state, the relevant matrix elements are those of a band problem in the Wigner-crystal Brillouin zone, closely analogous to the Adler–Wiser formulation of the dielectric response of periodic solids [1, 23]. In this work we evaluate the scalar longitudinal static response using the Hartree–Fock eigenvalues and plane-wave coefficients in the 𝐤+𝐆\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G} basis.

The converged Hartree–Fock eigenvalues and eigenvectors are used to compute the static density response of the insulating Wigner-crystal state. We consider a scalar longitudinal perturbation with wave vector 𝐪\mathbf{q}. For each initial momentum 𝐤\mathbf{k} in the first Wigner-crystal Brillouin zone, the final momentum is folded back to the same zone according to

𝐤𝐪=𝐤+𝐪−𝐆f​(𝐤,𝐪),𝐤𝐪∈1​B​Z,\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}=\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}),\qquad\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}\in\mathrm{1BZ}, (12)

where 𝐆f​(𝐤,𝐪)\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}) is a reciprocal-lattice vector of the Wigner-crystal. The corresponding density matrix element is

Mn​m(𝐤,𝐪)=⟨n𝐤|e−i𝐪⋅𝐫|m𝐤𝐪⟩=∑𝐆Zn​𝐆∗(𝐤)Zm,𝐆+𝐆f(𝐤𝐪).M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})=\left\langle n\mathbf{k}\left|e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\right|m\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}\right\rangle=\sum_{\mathbf{G}}Z^{*}_{n\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{k})Z_{m,\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}}}(\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}). (13)

Terms for which 𝐆+𝐆f\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}} lies outside the retained GG basis are omitted.

At zero temperature and for a fully spin-polarized insulating state, the static Hartree–Fock band polarizability is evaluated as

ΠHF​(𝐪,0)=1AW​∑𝐤w𝐤​∑n∈occ∑m∈emp|Mn​m​(𝐤,𝐪)|2​Δ​Em​n​(𝐤,𝐪)Δ​Em​n2​(𝐤,𝐪)+ηΠ2,\Pi_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0)=\frac{1}{A_{W}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}\sum_{n\in\mathrm{occ}}\sum_{m\in\mathrm{emp}}\left|M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})\right|^{2}\frac{\Delta E_{mn}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})}{\Delta E_{mn}^{2}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})+\eta_{\Pi}^{2}}, (14)

where

Δ​Em​n​(𝐤,𝐪)=εm​𝐤𝐪−εn​𝐤,\Delta E_{mn}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})=\varepsilon_{m\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}}-\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}, (15)

and ηΠ\eta_{\Pi} is a small numerical broadening. In the formal static limit one takes ηΠ→0+\eta_{\Pi}\rightarrow 0^{+}, so that Eq. (14) reduces to the usual interband Lindhard denominator 1/Δ​Em​n1/\Delta E_{mn}.

The static dielectric function is then defined as

εHF​(𝐪,0)=1+v~K​(q)​ΠHF​(𝐪,0),q=|𝐪|,\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0)=1+\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{K}}(q)\Pi_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0),\qquad q=|\mathbf{q}|, (16)

with v~K​(q)\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{K}}(q) given by Eq. (7). No additional spin-degeneracy factor is included, because the calculation is performed for a single fully spin-polarized occupied sector.

The insulating character of the self-consistent Wigner crystal fixes the long-wavelength limit. At 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{0}, orthonormality gives Mn​m​(𝐤,𝟎)=δn​mM_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{0})=\delta_{nm}, so the occupied–empty interband contribution vanishes and ΠHF​(𝟎,0)=0\Pi_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{0},0)=0. For small nonzero 𝐪\mathbf{q}, the interband form factor is linear in qq, hence ΠHF​(𝐪,0)∝q2\Pi_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0)\propto q^{2}. Since the two-dimensional Keldysh interaction behaves as v~K​(q)∝1/q\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{K}}(q)\propto 1/q for q→0q\rightarrow 0, Eq. (16) gives

εHF​(𝟎,0)=1,limq→0εHF​(𝐪,0)=1.\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{0},0)=1,\qquad\lim_{q\rightarrow 0}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0)=1. (17)

The derivation of the form factor and of the small-qq limit is given in SI.3

2.3 Triangular Wigner-crystal lattice and Brillouin-zone sampling

For an isotropic two-dimensional material with repulsive Coulomb-like interactions, the energetically favored Bravais lattice is triangular [4]. This motivates the use of a triangular Wigner-crystal primitive cell for the present TMD monolayer calculation, where low carrier density, large effective mass, and reduced dielectric screening provide a favorable setting for Wigner crystallization [14].

We denote the real-space primitive vectors of the Wigner crystal by 𝐚1\mathbf{a}_{1} and 𝐚2\mathbf{a}_{2} and choose their orientation such that the Wigner-crystal primitive-cell area is AW=𝐳^⋅(𝐚1×𝐚2)>0.A_{W}=\hat{\mathbf{z}}\cdot\left(\mathbf{a}_{1}\times\mathbf{a}_{2}\right)>0. The corresponding reciprocal primitive vectors are 𝐛1=(2​π/AW)​(𝐚2×𝐳^)\mathbf{b}_{1}=(2\pi/A_{W})(\mathbf{a}_{2}\times\hat{\mathbf{z}}) and 𝐛2=(2​π/AW)​(𝐳^×𝐚1)\mathbf{b}_{2}=(2\pi/A_{W})(\hat{\mathbf{z}}\times\mathbf{a}_{1}). A general reciprocal-lattice vector is then written in Miller form as 𝐆m​n=m​𝐛1+n​𝐛2,m,n∈ℤ\mathbf{G}_{mn}=m\mathbf{b}_{1}+n\mathbf{b}_{2},\qquad m,n\in\mathbb{Z}.

We use this hexagonal Brillouin zone as the fundamental momentum-space cell for the Hartree–Fock band structure. The standard high-symmetry points are denoted by Γ\Gamma at the zone center, MM at the midpoint of a hexagon edge, and KK at a hexagon corner. The single-particle states are labeled by a reduced crystal momentum 𝐤\mathbf{k} inside this first Brillouin zone and by reciprocal-lattice vectors 𝐆\mathbf{G}, leading to the 𝐤+𝐆\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G} plane-wave representation used below. The Brillouin-zone sampling is performed in the irreducible Γ\Gamma–KK–MM wedge of the hexagonal zone as shown in Figure 1.

The plane-wave basis is truncated by retaining a symmetry-compatible star of reciprocal vectors. The retained set is selected by a using a circular cutoff in Cartesian reciprocal space, (𝒢cut=𝐆m​n:|𝐆m​n|2≤Gcut2).(\mathcal{G}_{\mathrm{cut}}={\mathbf{G}_{mn}:|\mathbf{G}_{mn}|^{2}\leq G_{\mathrm{cut}}^{2}}). This radial cutoff makes the accepted set a union of complete stars under the point group D6D_{6} of the hexagonal Brillouin zone. Further details on the geometry of the triangular Wigner-crystal lattice are provided in Sec. SI.4.

The Hartree–Fock band structure is obtained by diagonalizing the matrix Hamiltonian at the representative 𝐤\mathbf{k} points of the irreducible Γ\Gamma–KK–MM wedge. For the exchange term, however, the source momentum sum is evaluated over the full Brillouin-zone mesh. This full mesh is generated from the wedge representatives by applying the distinct symmetry images. Thus the target momenta are represented in the irreducible wedge, while the exchange field is evaluated by an explicit full-zone summation. A symmetry-reduced wedge form of the same exchange sum is possible and is described in  SI.5, but it is not used in the production results reported here.

3 Numerical code and results

3.1 Numerical workflow and convergence

The reciprocal-lattice basis is selected by a circular cutoff in |𝐆|2|\mathbf{G}|^{2}, which preserves complete D6D_{6} stars of the triangular Wigner-crystal reciprocal lattice. The Brillouin-zone sampling is performed in the irreducible Γ\Gamma–KK–MM wedge, while full-zone symmetry images are reconstructed when required for the exchange matrix and for the dielectric form factors. The code supports Coulomb, Keldysh, and Stern-family interaction kernels; the production results reported below use the Keldysh interaction appropriate for 2D TMD monolayer. A special numerical treatment is required for the singular q=0q=0 component of the Coulomb and Keldysh interactions entering the Hartree–Fock matrix elements. In the production calculations we replace the singular value by the analytic average of the interaction over a small circular cell of radius qcq_{c} around the origin in reciprocal space,

v¯​(0)=1π​qc2​∫|𝐪|≤qcd2​q​v~​(q).\overline{v}(0)=\frac{1}{\pi q_{c}^{2}}\int_{|\mathbf{q}|\leq q_{c}}d^{2}q\,\widetilde{v}(q). (18)

For the Keldysh interaction in Eq. (7), the cell average gives

v¯K​(0)=4​π​e2ε​qc2​ρ0​ln⁡(1+ρ0​qc).\overline{v}_{K}(0)=\frac{4\pi e^{2}}{\varepsilon q_{c}^{2}\rho_{0}}\ln(1+\rho_{0}q_{c}). (19)

For q>qcq>q_{c}, the unmodified interaction v~K​(q)\widetilde{v}_{K}(q) is used. This replacement is applied only to the singular Coulomb/Keldysh kernels. A genuine Stern-screened interaction is finite at q=0q=0 and is therefore evaluated directly.

The self-consistent cycle proceeds as follows. Starting from a periodic Gaussian density with the Wigner-crystal periodicity, the Hartree matrix is built from the density harmonics ηW​(𝐐)\eta_{W}(\mathbf{Q}). After a short Hartree warm-up, the exchange matrix is evaluated from the occupied Hartree–Fock eigenvectors and the matrix Hamiltonian is diagonalized at each representative wedge momentum. The updated eigenvectors are then used to reconstruct the density harmonics, closing the self-consistency loop. Convergence is monitored through the change of ηW​(𝐐)\eta_{W}(\mathbf{Q}), the stability of the total energy, and the regularity of the band structure at high-symmetry points.

The main numerical parameters are summarized in Table S1 in Sec. SI.4. The convergence of the results was checked against the number of retained reciprocal vectors, the wedge mesh density, the number of empty bands retained in the polarizability, and the broadening parameter ηΠ\eta_{\Pi} entering Eq. (14).

The Hartree-only part of the self-consistent problem can possess more than one numerical attractor for the same initial parameter set. This is expected in a broken-symmetry calculation, where different preconditioned density patterns may be stabilized before exchange is activated. In the production calculation, the Hartree warm-up is used only as a stabilizing stage for the subsequent Hartree–Fock iteration, not as an independent physical solution. When more than one Hartree-preconditioned branch was obtained, the branch retained for the Hartree–Fock calculation was selected by three criteria: preservation of the triangular Wigner-crystal symmetry in the density, regularity of the band structure after exchange is included, and recovery of the expected degeneracy pattern at the high-symmetry points of the hexagonal Brillouin zone. The alternative branch was discarded because it led to an irregular Hartree–Fock spectrum and to a density pattern inconsistent with the intended triangular Wigner-crystal solution.

3.2 Band, density, and dielectric signatures of Wigner-crystal order

We characterize the converged Hartree–Fock solution using three complementary signatures of Wigner-crystal order: the symmetry structure of the band spectrum, the amplitude of the first density harmonics, and the static dielectric response. These quantities are not used as a thermodynamic proof of a liquid–crystal transition, but as phase-sensitive indicators of the crystalline character of the self-consistent solution at a given rsr_{s}.

The calculated band structure provides a sensitive spectral signature of triangular Wigner-crystal order. At the high-symmetry points Γ\Gamma, KK, and MM, the Hartree–Fock bands are constrained by the little groups of the corresponding momenta and are expected to exhibit the associated degeneracy structure and regularity. As the density increases, equivalently as rsr_{s} decreases, the system approaches the weak-crystal or liquid side. In this regime, the self-consistent crystalline solution is expected to become less robust, and the high-symmetry band signatures may become less sharply defined.

The strength of the Wigner-crystal density modulation is estimated by the first-star order parameter

M1=1|ηW​(𝟎)|​16​∑𝐐∈𝒮1|ηW​(𝐐)|,M_{1}=\frac{1}{|\eta_{W}(\mathbf{0})|}\frac{1}{6}\sum_{\mathbf{Q}\in\mathcal{S}_{1}}\left|\eta_{W}(\mathbf{Q})\right|, (20)

where ηW​(𝐐)\eta_{W}(\mathbf{Q}) are the Fourier coefficients of the charge density and 𝒮1\mathcal{S}_{1} denotes the six shortest nonzero reciprocal-lattice vectors of the triangular Wigner crystal. The normalization by |ηW​(𝟎)||\eta_{W}(\mathbf{0})| removes the overall density scale, so that M1M_{1} measures the relative amplitude of the fundamental density modulation. The first-star harmonics are the most relevant components for characterizing crystalline order because they are the longest-wavelength Fourier components compatible with the triangular broken-symmetry pattern. They therefore appear first at the onset of density modulation and are less sensitive than higher harmonics to short-range details of the charge profile. Accordingly, M1≃0M_{1}\simeq 0 signals a nearly uniform or weakly modulated density, whereas a finite M1M_{1} indicates a Wigner-crystal-like density modulation.

The static dielectric function provides a complementary response signature of the converged state. It is evaluated from the Hartree–Fock band polarizability introduced in Sec. 2.2. For each wave vector 𝐪\mathbf{q}, the numerical implementation folds 𝐤+𝐪\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q} back to the first Wigner-crystal Brillouin zone, evaluates the density form factor Mn​m​(𝐤,𝐪)M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}) from the converged eigenvectors, and sums over occupied–empty band pairs. The same reconstructed full-zone representation used in the exchange calculation is used to ensure that the folding operation and the GG-index shift in the form factor are treated consistently. The resulting dielectric function is checked against the long-wavelength constraints derived in Sec. 2.2, εHF​(𝟎,0)=1\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{0},0)=1 and limq→0εHF​(𝐪,0)=1\lim_{q\to 0}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0)=1, which test the consistency of the numerical folding procedure and occupied–empty band summation.

3.3 Spin channels and exchange scaling

The self-consistent calculation used for the main Wigner-crystal solution is fully spin polarized. In this case the occupied background contains a single spin component and the same-spin particle spectrum is obtained from

h𝐆𝐆′SC​(𝐤)=T𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤)+V𝐆𝐆′H−X𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤),h^{\mathrm{SC}}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})=T_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})+V^{H}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}-X_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}), (21)

where X𝐆𝐆′X_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}} is the positive exchange matrix built from the occupied spin-polarized Hartree–Fock state. The spin-reversed particle spectrum is obtained in the frozen Hartree potential of the same converged density, but without exchange with the occupied background, (Σ𝐆𝐆′F,σ​(𝐤)→0\Sigma^{F,\sigma}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})\to 0 in Eq. (21)).

For comparison, a restricted unpolarized estimate can be generated by scaling the exchange matrix by one half,

h𝐆𝐆′unpol​(𝐤)≈T𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤)+V𝐆𝐆′H−12​X𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤).h^{\mathrm{unpol}}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})\approx T_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})+V^{H}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{2}X_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}). (22)

This approximation corresponds to assuming equal spin densities, ρ↑=ρ↓=ρ/2\rho_{\uparrow}=\rho_{\downarrow}=\rho/2, while keeping the same total Hartree density. It should not be confused with a fully self-consistent two-spin Hartree–Fock calculation.

In the present work we restrict the quantitative analysis to the fully spin-polarized case, for which the Hartree–Fock exchange field is treated self-consistently within a single occupied spin sector. The same formulation also provides a controlled way to analyze spin-reversed frozen-density excitations, where the Hartree potential is kept fixed and the same-spin exchange term is absent. By contrast, a genuine unpolarized Wigner crystal requires a self-consistent two-spin Hartree–Fock treatment, including the coupled evolution of the two spin densities and their same-spin exchange fields. This more complex case is currently under investigation and will be addressed separately.

3.4 Band-structure results

Figure 2 summarizes a representative fully spin-polarized Hartree–Fock Wigner-crystal solution. The panels show the evolution from the initial crystalline density used to start the self-consistent iteration to the converged charge density, followed by the corresponding same-spin Hartree–Fock band structure and the static dielectric function. This arrangement emphasizes the numerical sequence of the calculation: initialization, self-consistent crystalline solution, quasiparticle spectrum, and density response.

The numerical spectra display the singlet and doublet structures expected from the point-group symmetry of the hexagonal Wigner-crystal Brillouin zone. In particular, the bands remain regular near Γ\Gamma, show the appropriate degeneracy structure near the zone corners, and evolve smoothly along the Γ\Gamma–KK–MM path. The charge-density and band-structure panels in Fig. 2 are consistent with this diagnostic picture. At larger rsr_{s}, the converged density is more strongly modulated and the Hartree–Fock spectrum displays clearer crystalline band features. As rsr_{s} decreases, the density modulation weakens, the order parameter M1M_{1} decreases, and the crystalline Hartree–Fock solution becomes less robust. This behavior indicates a loss of Wigner-crystal character and suggests that the system is approaching the weak-crystal or liquid side, although a thermodynamic identification of the transition would require an energy comparison or an independent phase-stability analysis.

The values of the first-star order parameter included in Fig. 2 provide a quantitative measure of the density modulation visible in the charge-density panels. For the converged Hartree–Fock solutions, M1finM_{1}^{\mathrm{fin}} increases overall with rsr_{s}, from M1fin=0.100M_{1}^{\mathrm{fin}}=0.100 at rs=4r_{s}=4 to M1fin=0.586M_{1}^{\mathrm{fin}}=0.586 at rs=50r_{s}=50. This trend confirms that the self-consistent solution becomes increasingly Wigner-crystal-like in the dilute regime: as the lattice constant increases and the carrier density decreases, the charge density becomes more localized around the triangular lattice sites, and the Fourier weight at the first reciprocal-lattice star increases.

A complementary real-space measure of the density modulation is provided by the density-contrast ratio Cn=nmax/nminC_{n}=n_{\max}/n_{\min}, where nmaxn_{\max} and nminn_{\min} are the maximum and minimum values of the converged charge density within one Wigner-crystal unit cell. While M1M_{1} measures the weight of the fundamental Fourier harmonics, CnC_{n} directly quantifies the ripple character of the real-space density profile. Values of CnC_{n} close to unity correspond to a nearly uniform density, whereas larger values indicate a stronger spatial separation between density maxima at the lattice sites and density minima in the interstitial regions. Thus, the combined behavior of M1M_{1} and CnC_{n} provides a more complete characterization of the Wigner-crystal modulation.

The comparison between the initial and final values also shows that the self-consistent calculation is not merely preserving the imposed starting configuration. For example, at rs=30r_{s}=30 the initial state has a larger first-star amplitude, M1ini=0.668M_{1}^{\mathrm{ini}}=0.668, whereas the converged solution relaxes to M1fin=0.504M_{1}^{\mathrm{fin}}=0.504. This reduction is consistent with the visual density map, where the final density is less sharply localized than the initial Gaussian configuration. Thus M1M_{1} acts as a useful internal consistency check: the converged value reflects the self-consistent Hartree–Fock balance between kinetic energy, Hartree repulsion, and exchange, rather than the artificial degree of localization chosen in the initialization.

3.5 Static dielectric-function results

The static dielectric functions shown in Fig. 2 exhibit a systematic reduction of their maximum value with increasing rsr_{s}. According to the definition of εHF​(q,0)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0) introduced in Sec. 2.2, the screened interaction may be written as

v~scr​(q)=v~K​(q)εHF​(q,0).\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{scr}}(q)=\frac{\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{K}}(q)}{\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0)}. (23)

Here v~K​(q)\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{K}}(q) is the bare Keldysh interaction, including the background dielectric environment, whereas εHF​(q,0)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0) describes the additional finite-qq screening generated by the resident carriers in the Hartree–Fock Wigner-crystal state. Thus larger values of εHF​(q,0)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0) correspond to a stronger reduction of the effective electron–electron interaction at the corresponding momentum transfer.

The decrease of the peak value of εHF​(q,0)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0) with increasing rsr_{s} reflects the reduction of the electronic polarizability in the dilute Wigner crystal. As rsr_{s} increases, the Wigner-crystal lattice constant increases and the carrier density decreases. The electrons become more localized, the overlap between neighboring density modulations is reduced, and the finite-qq Hartree–Fock polarizability is weakened. Consequently the maximum of εHF​(q,0)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0) moves closer to unity, indicating that the resident carriers become less efficient at screening an external perturbation and that the effective interaction approaches the bare Keldysh interaction. The momentum at which the maximum occurs gives the most efficient static-screening momentum channel; its physical interpretation and its scaling with the Wigner-crystal reciprocal-lattice scale are discussed in SI.6.

4 Conclusions

Experimentally isolating spin/valley-polarized Wigner-crystal spectra is challenging. A possible test of the present predictions for monolayer WSe2 would be a time-resolved, helicity-resolved optical spectroscopy experiment on an hBN-encapsulated, gate-tunable WSe2 monolayer. In such a protocol, a resident-electron Wigner crystal in the relevant density range would first be driven toward a nearly spin/valley-polarized configuration by resonant circular optical pumping. Efficient optical spin/valley pumping of resident electrons has already been demonstrated in nn-doped WSe2 and WS2 monolayers [12], and recent Wigner-polaron experiments suggest that optical control of spin/valley degrees of freedom in the Wigner crystal regime is experimentally accessible [25]. The degree of polarization could be calibrated independently by Faraday-geometry magneto-optical measurements of the valley-Zeeman splitting in an out-of-plane magnetic field [15]. Such an experiment, performed on a prepared spin/valley-polarized configuration, would primarily test the spin-conserving, frozen-spin/valley sector of the polarized Hartree–Fock calculation. The present work connects the conventional theory of the low-density 2D Wigner crystal with recent optical studies of charge order in atomically thin semiconductors. The triangular Wigner crystal and its collective properties have long been established as central features of the dilute 2D electron gas [4, 17]. Recent experiments on charge-tunable TMD monolayers have shown that Wigner-crystal charge order can be accessed optically even in zero magnetic field, through exciton-umklapp signatures and related resonances [13]. More recent work has further emphasized that exciton spectroscopy can probe not only the static periodic potential of the Wigner crystal, but also dynamical electron-lattice excitations in the form of Wigner-polaron resonances [20, 25, 2]. These developments motivate a microscopic calculation that is adapted to the Keldysh interaction and optical response of a monolayer TMD.

Within this context, the main physical contribution of the present work is the self-consistent Hartree–Fock construction of a spin-polarized Wigner-crystal state in monolayer WSe2, together with the corresponding quasiparticle band structure and finite-momentum static dielectric response. The calculation connects, within the same microscopic framework, the real-space crystalline density, the Hartree–Fock spectrum in the Wigner-crystal Brillouin zone, the first-star density order parameter M1M_{1}, the density-contrast ratio CnC_{n}, and the band-based dielectric function εHF​(q,0)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0). The results show that increasing rsr_{s} strengthens the crystalline density modulation while reducing the additional electronic screening produced by the resident carriers. This is the expected behavior of a dilute Wigner crystal: the electrons become more localized in real space, and their finite-qq polarizability becomes less efficient.

The conclusions should be understood within the scope of the approximation. The regularity of the band structure, the evolution of M1M_{1}, and the behavior of εHF​(q,0)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0) are used here as complementary signatures of the self-consistent crystalline Hartree–Fock solution. They do not by themselves constitute a thermodynamic proof of the liquid–crystal transition, which would require an energy comparison or an independent phase-stability analysis. Nevertheless, the combined density, band-structure, and dielectric-response diagnostics provide a consistent microscopic picture of the evolution from a weakly crystalline solution toward a more localized Wigner-crystal state.

The numerical implementation is also flexible enough to support systematic convergence checks. In particular, the kk-mesh density can be increased without changing the structure of the calculation, allowing the high-symmetry band features and the finite-qq dielectric response to be tested on progressively denser Brillouin-zone grids. The code uses an irreducible Γ\Gamma–KK–MM wedge for the self-consistent calculation and reconstructs the full Brillouin zone when required for exchange and dielectric matrix elements. This capability is important for future refinements, including denser momentum sampling, larger plane-wave bases, alternative interaction kernels, and extensions toward unpolarized, multiband, finite-temperature, or collective-mode calculations.

The numerical code used in this work is a research version developed for the present calculations; it is not yet distributed as a public software package, but can be made available from the authors upon reasonable request.

SI.1 Hartree–Fock matrix elements in the 𝐤+𝐆\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G} representation

This section gives the coordinate-space starting point and the explicit projection leading to the matrix elements used in Sec. 2.1. The Hartree–Fock equation in coordinate representation is

∫d2​r′​HHF​(𝐫,𝐫′)​ψn​𝐤​σ​(𝐫′)=εn​𝐤​σ​ψn​𝐤​σ​(𝐫),\int d^{2}r^{\prime}\,H_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\psi_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}\psi_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}), (S1)

where, in the absence of an external potential,

HHF​(𝐫,𝐫′)=[hband​(𝐫)+VH​(𝐫)]​δ​(𝐫−𝐫′)−ΣFσ​(𝐫,𝐫′).H_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\left[h_{\mathrm{band}}(\mathbf{r})+V_{H}(\mathbf{r})\right]\delta(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})-\Sigma_{F}^{\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}). (S2)

Here hbandh_{\mathrm{band}} is the effective band-edge operator, VHV_{H} is the Hartree potential, and ΣFσ\Sigma_{F}^{\sigma} is the spin-dependent Fock exchange operator. The local Hartree potential is

VH​(𝐫)=∫d2​r′​v​(𝐫−𝐫′)​n​(𝐫′),V_{H}(\mathbf{r})=\int d^{2}r^{\prime}\,v(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})n(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}), (S3)

whereas the exchange kernel is

ΣFσ​(𝐫,𝐫′)=v⁡(𝐫−𝐫′)​ρσ​(𝐫,𝐫′).\Sigma_{F}^{\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=v(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})\rho_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime}). (S4)

The spin-resolved one-body density matrix is

ρσ​(𝐫,𝐫′)=∑n∈occ∑𝐤w𝐤​ψn​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)​ψn​𝐤​σ∗​(𝐫′),\rho_{\sigma}(\mathbf{r},\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\sum_{n\in\mathrm{occ}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}\psi_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})\psi^{*}_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r}^{\prime}), (S5)

where w𝐤w_{\mathbf{k}} are the Brillouin-zone integration weights.

Since the Wigner-crystal state is periodic with respect to the emergent triangular lattice, the single-particle orbitals are expanded as

ψn​𝐤​σ​(𝐫)=∑𝐆Zn​𝐆​σ​(𝐤)​1A​ei⁡(𝐤+𝐆)⋅𝐫,\psi_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{G}}Z_{n\mathbf{G}\sigma}(\mathbf{k})\frac{1}{\sqrt{A}}e^{i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}}, (S6)

where A=Nc​AWA=N_{c}A_{W} is the total normalization area, AWA_{W} is the real-space Wigner-crystal primitive-cell area, and NcN_{c} is the number of Wigner cells in the Born–von Karman supercell. Equivalently,

|ψn​𝐤​σ⟩=∑𝐆Zn​𝐆​σ(𝐤)|𝐤+𝐆⟩.\left|\psi_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}\right\rangle=\sum_{\mathbf{G}}Z_{n\mathbf{G}\sigma}(\mathbf{k})\left|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}\right\rangle. (S7)

Projecting Eq. (S1) onto ⟨𝐤+𝐆|\left\langle\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}\right| gives

∑𝐆′⟨𝐤+𝐆​|HHF|​𝐤+𝐆′⟩​Zn​𝐆′​σ​(𝐤)=εn​𝐤​σ​Zn​𝐆​σ​(𝐤).\sum_{\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}\left\langle\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}\left|H_{\mathrm{HF}}\right|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}\right\rangle Z_{n\mathbf{G}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{k})=\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}Z_{n\mathbf{G}\sigma}(\mathbf{k}). (S8)

Defining

h𝐆𝐆′σ​(𝐤)=⟨𝐤+𝐆​|HHF|​𝐤+𝐆′⟩,h_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}^{\sigma}(\mathbf{k})=\left\langle\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}\left|H_{\mathrm{HF}}\right|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}\right\rangle, (S9)

one obtains the matrix eigenvalue problem

∑𝐆′h𝐆𝐆′σ​(𝐤)​Zn​𝐆′​σ​(𝐤)=εn​𝐤​σ​Zn​𝐆​σ​(𝐤).\sum_{\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}h_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}^{\sigma}(\mathbf{k})Z_{n\mathbf{G}^{\prime}\sigma}(\mathbf{k})=\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}\sigma}Z_{n\mathbf{G}\sigma}(\mathbf{k}). (S10)

hband=−ℏ22​m∗​∇2.h_{\mathrm{band}}=-\frac{\hbar^{2}}{2m^{*}}\nabla^{2}. (S11)

The plane waves are eigenstates of this operator. Therefore, the kinetic contribution is diagonal in the 𝐆\mathbf{G} index,

T𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤)=ℏ2​|𝐤+𝐆|22​m∗​δ𝐆𝐆′.T_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})=\frac{\hbar^{2}|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}|^{2}}{2m^{*}}\delta_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}. (S12)

The Hartree potential is periodic with the Wigner-crystal lattice and can be expanded as

VH​(𝐫)=∑𝐐VH​(𝐐)​ei​𝐐⋅𝐫.V_{H}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{Q}}V_{H}(\mathbf{Q})e^{i\mathbf{Q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}. (S13)

Using the normalized plane-wave representation,

⟨𝐫|𝐤+𝐆⟩=1A​ei⁡(𝐤+𝐆)⋅𝐫,\left\langle\mathbf{r}\middle|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}\right\rangle=\frac{1}{\sqrt{A}}e^{i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}}, (S14)

the Hartree matrix element is

V𝐆𝐆′H\displaystyle V^{H}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}} =⟨𝐤+𝐆​|VH|​𝐤+𝐆′⟩\displaystyle=\left\langle\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}\left|V_{H}\right|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}\right\rangle
=∑𝐐VH​(𝐐)​1A​∫Ad2​r​ei⁡(𝐐+𝐆′−𝐆)⋅𝐫.\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{Q}}V_{H}(\mathbf{Q})\frac{1}{A}\int_{A}d^{2}r\,e^{i(\mathbf{Q}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}-\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}}. (S15)

The integral gives the reciprocal-lattice selection rule

1A​∫Ad2​r​ei⁡(𝐐+𝐆′−𝐆)⋅𝐫=δ𝐐,𝐆−𝐆′.\frac{1}{A}\int_{A}d^{2}r\,e^{i(\mathbf{Q}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}-\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}}=\delta_{\mathbf{Q},\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}. (S16)

Therefore

V𝐆𝐆′H=VH​(𝐆−𝐆′).V^{H}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}=V_{H}(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}^{\prime}). (S17)

The Hartree potential is the convolution of the interaction with the density. In reciprocal space this gives

VH​(𝐐)=v~​(𝐐)​n​(𝐐),V_{H}(\mathbf{Q})=\widetilde{v}(\mathbf{Q})n(\mathbf{Q}), (S18)

and hence

V𝐆𝐆′H=v~​(𝐆−𝐆′)​n​(𝐆−𝐆′).V^{H}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}=\widetilde{v}(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}^{\prime})n(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}^{\prime}). (S19)

This contribution is independent of 𝐤\mathbf{k}. The Fock matrix element is

Σ𝐆𝐆′F,σ​(𝐤)=⟨𝐤+𝐆​|ΣFσ|​𝐤+𝐆′⟩.\Sigma_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}^{F,\sigma}(\mathbf{k})=\left\langle\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}\left|\Sigma_{F}^{\sigma}\right|\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}\right\rangle. (S20)

Substituting Eqs. (S4) and (S5), and using the expansion in Eq. (S6), gives

Σ𝐆𝐆′F,σ​(𝐤)\displaystyle\Sigma_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}^{F,\sigma}(\mathbf{k}) =∑n′∈occ∑𝐤′w𝐤′​∑𝐆1,𝐆2Zn′​𝐆1​σ​(𝐤′)​Zn′​𝐆2​σ∗​(𝐤′)\displaystyle=\sum_{n^{\prime}\in\mathrm{occ}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}w_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}_{1},\mathbf{G}_{2}}Z_{n^{\prime}\mathbf{G}_{1}\sigma}(\mathbf{k}^{\prime})Z^{*}_{n^{\prime}\mathbf{G}_{2}\sigma}(\mathbf{k}^{\prime})
×I⁡(𝐆,𝐆′,𝐤,𝐤′,𝐆1,𝐆2),\displaystyle\quad\times I(\mathbf{G},\mathbf{G}^{\prime};\mathbf{k},\mathbf{k}^{\prime};\mathbf{G}_{1},\mathbf{G}_{2}), (S21)

where

I\displaystyle I =∫d2​r​d2​r′​v​(𝐫−𝐫′)​ei⁡[(𝐤′+𝐆1)−(𝐤+𝐆)]⋅𝐫​ei⁡[(𝐤+𝐆′)−(𝐤′+𝐆2)]⋅𝐫′.\displaystyle=\int d^{2}r\,d^{2}r^{\prime}\,v(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})e^{i[(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}+\mathbf{G}_{1})-(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})]\cdot\mathbf{r}}e^{i[(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime})-(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}+\mathbf{G}_{2})]\cdot\mathbf{r}^{\prime}}. (S22)

The interaction is Fourier transformed as

v⁡(𝐫−𝐫′)=∫d2​q(2​π)2​v~​(𝐪)​ei​𝐪⋅(𝐫−𝐫′).v(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})=\int\frac{d^{2}q}{(2\pi)^{2}}\widetilde{v}(\mathbf{q})e^{i\mathbf{q}\cdot(\mathbf{r}-\mathbf{r}^{\prime})}. (S23)

The integrations over 𝐫\mathbf{r} and 𝐫′\mathbf{r}^{\prime} impose

𝐪=(𝐤+𝐆)−(𝐤′+𝐆1),𝐆−𝐆′=𝐆1−𝐆2.\mathbf{q}=(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})-(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}+\mathbf{G}_{1}),\qquad\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}^{\prime}=\mathbf{G}_{1}-\mathbf{G}_{2}. (S24)

Thus

I=v~​[(𝐤+𝐆)−(𝐤′+𝐆1)]​δ𝐆−𝐆′,𝐆1−𝐆2.I=\widetilde{v}\!\left[(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})-(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}+\mathbf{G}_{1})\right]\delta_{\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}^{\prime},\,\mathbf{G}_{1}-\mathbf{G}_{2}}. (S25)

Using the selection rule to eliminate 𝐆2\mathbf{G}_{2}, the exchange matrix becomes

Σ𝐆𝐆′F,σ​(𝐤)\displaystyle\Sigma_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}^{F,\sigma}(\mathbf{k}) =∑n′∈occ∑𝐤′w𝐤′​∑𝐆1Zn′​𝐆1​σ​(𝐤′)​Zn′,𝐆1−𝐆+𝐆′,σ∗​(𝐤′)\displaystyle=\sum_{n^{\prime}\in\mathrm{occ}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}w_{\mathbf{k}^{\prime}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}_{1}}Z_{n^{\prime}\mathbf{G}_{1}\sigma}(\mathbf{k}^{\prime})Z^{*}_{n^{\prime},\mathbf{G}_{1}-\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime},\sigma}(\mathbf{k}^{\prime})
×v~​[(𝐤+𝐆)−(𝐤′+𝐆1)].\displaystyle\quad\times\widetilde{v}\!\left[(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})-(\mathbf{k}^{\prime}+\mathbf{G}_{1})\right]. (S26)

Terms for which the shifted reciprocal vector 𝐆1−𝐆+𝐆′\mathbf{G}_{1}-\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime} lies outside the retained plane-wave basis are omitted.

Combining the kinetic, Hartree, and Fock terms gives

h𝐆𝐆′σ​(𝐤)=T𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤)+V𝐆𝐆′H−Σ𝐆𝐆′F,σ​(𝐤).h_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}^{\sigma}(\mathbf{k})=T_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})+V^{H}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}-\Sigma_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}^{F,\sigma}(\mathbf{k}). (S27)

For the spin-polarized Wigner crystal considered in the main text, only one spin sector is occupied, and the exchange contribution is present only in the same-spin particle channel.

SI.2 Initial density harmonics ηW(0)​(𝐐)\eta_{W}^{(0)}(\mathbf{Q})

The relation between the initial coefficients F𝐤(0)​(𝐆)F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{G}) and the initial density harmonics ηW(0)​(𝐐)\eta_{W}^{(0)}(\mathbf{Q}) follows directly from the density associated with the cell-periodic part of the Bloch state. Since the overall phase factor ei​𝐤⋅𝐫e^{i\mathbf{k}\cdot\mathbf{r}} cancels in the density, we define

u𝐤(0)​(𝐫)=∑𝐆F𝐤(0)​(𝐆)​ei​𝐆⋅𝐫.u_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{G}}F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{G})e^{i\mathbf{G}\cdot\mathbf{r}}. (S28)

The initial density is written as the Brillouin-zone average

n(0)​(𝐫)=1AW​∑𝐤w𝐤​|u𝐤(0)​(𝐫)|2,n^{(0)}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{A_{W}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}\left|u_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{r})\right|^{2}, (S29)

with ∑𝐤w𝐤=1\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}=1. Substituting the plane-wave expansion of u𝐤(0)​(𝐫)u_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{r}) gives

n(0)​(𝐫)\displaystyle n^{(0)}(\mathbf{r}) =1AW∑𝐤w𝐤∑𝐆,𝐆′F𝐤(0)(𝐆)F𝐤(0)∗(𝐆′)ei⁡(𝐆−𝐆′)⋅𝐫.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{A_{W}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}\sum_{\mathbf{G},\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{G})F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)*}(\mathbf{G}^{\prime})e^{i(\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}^{\prime})\cdot\mathbf{r}}. (S30)

Comparing this expression with

n(0)​(𝐫)=∑𝐐ηW(0)​(𝐐)​ei​𝐐⋅𝐫,n^{(0)}(\mathbf{r})=\sum_{\mathbf{Q}}\eta_{W}^{(0)}(\mathbf{Q})e^{i\mathbf{Q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}, (S31)

one obtains

ηW(0)(𝐐)=1AW∑𝐤w𝐤∑𝐆F𝐤(0)∗(𝐆)F𝐤(0)(𝐆+𝐐).\eta_{W}^{(0)}(\mathbf{Q})=\frac{1}{A_{W}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}}F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)*}(\mathbf{G})F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{Q}). (S32)

For the real Gaussian initialization used in the code, this becomes

ηW(0)​(𝐐)=1AW​∑𝐤w𝐤​∑𝐆F𝐤(0)​(𝐆)​F𝐤(0)​(𝐆+𝐐).\eta_{W}^{(0)}(\mathbf{Q})=\frac{1}{A_{W}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}}F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{G})F_{\mathbf{k}}^{(0)}(\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{Q}). (S33)

For a uniform full-BZ mesh, w𝐤=1/Nkw_{\mathbf{k}}=1/N_{k}, so Eq. (S33) is identical to the explicit 1/(AW​Nk)1/(A_{W}N_{k}) expression.

SI.3 Static Hartree–Fock band polarizability

The density response is computed from the converged Hartree–Fock eigenvalues and eigenvectors in the 𝐤+𝐆\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G} basis. The Bloch states are

ψn​𝐤​(𝐫)=1A​∑𝐆Zn​𝐆​(𝐤)​ei⁡(𝐤+𝐆)⋅𝐫.\psi_{n\mathbf{k}}(\mathbf{r})=\frac{1}{\sqrt{A}}\sum_{\mathbf{G}}Z_{n\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{k})e^{i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}}. (S34)

For a perturbing wave vector 𝐪\mathbf{q}, the final momentum is folded back into the first Wigner-crystal Brillouin zone,

𝐤𝐪=𝐤+𝐪−𝐆f​(𝐤,𝐪),𝐤𝐪∈1​B​Z,\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}=\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}),\qquad\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}\in\mathrm{1BZ}, (S35)

where 𝐆f\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}} is a reciprocal-lattice vector. The density matrix element is

Mn​m​(𝐤,𝐪)\displaystyle M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q}) =⟨n𝐤|e−i𝐪⋅𝐫|m𝐤𝐪⟩\displaystyle=\left\langle n\mathbf{k}\left|e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}\right|m\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}\right\rangle
=∑𝐆,𝐆′Zn​𝐆∗(𝐤)Zm​𝐆′(𝐤𝐪)1A∫Ad2re−i(𝐤+𝐆)⋅𝐫e−i𝐪⋅𝐫ei⁡(𝐤𝐪+𝐆′)⋅𝐫.\displaystyle=\sum_{\mathbf{G},\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}Z^{*}_{n\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{k})Z_{m\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}})\frac{1}{A}\int_{A}d^{2}r\,e^{-i(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})\cdot\mathbf{r}}e^{-i\mathbf{q}\cdot\mathbf{r}}e^{i(\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime})\cdot\mathbf{r}}. (S36)

Using Eq. (S35), the phase in the integral is

𝐤𝐪+𝐆′−𝐪−𝐤−𝐆=𝐆′−𝐆−𝐆f.\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}-\mathbf{q}-\mathbf{k}-\mathbf{G}=\mathbf{G}^{\prime}-\mathbf{G}-\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}}. (S37)

Therefore the plane-wave integral imposes the reciprocal-lattice selection rule

𝐆′=𝐆+𝐆f,\mathbf{G}^{\prime}=\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}}, (S38)

and the form factor becomes

Mn​m​(𝐤,𝐪)=∑𝐆Zn​𝐆∗​(𝐤)​Zm,𝐆+𝐆f​(𝐤𝐪).M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})=\sum_{\mathbf{G}}Z^{*}_{n\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{k})Z_{m,\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}}}(\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}). (S39)

Terms for which 𝐆+𝐆f\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}} is outside the retained plane-wave basis are omitted in the numerical implementation.

With the convention used in the main text, the positive static polarizability is the negative of the usual static density-response function. For a fully spin-polarized insulator at zero temperature it can be written as an occupied–empty interband sum,

ΠHF​(𝐪,0)=1AW​∑𝐤w𝐤​∑n∈occ∑m∈emp|Mn​m​(𝐤,𝐪)|2​Δ​Em​n​(𝐤,𝐪)Δ​Em​n2​(𝐤,𝐪)+ηΠ2,\Pi_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0)=\frac{1}{A_{W}}\sum_{\mathbf{k}}w_{\mathbf{k}}\sum_{n\in\mathrm{occ}}\sum_{m\in\mathrm{emp}}\left|M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})\right|^{2}\frac{\Delta E_{mn}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})}{\Delta E_{mn}^{2}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})+\eta_{\Pi}^{2}}, (S40)

where

Δ​Em​n​(𝐤,𝐪)=εm​𝐤𝐪−εn​𝐤.\Delta E_{mn}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})=\varepsilon_{m\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}}-\varepsilon_{n\mathbf{k}}. (S41)

The parameter ηΠ\eta_{\Pi} is a small numerical broadening. In the analytic static limit, ηΠ→0+\eta_{\Pi}\rightarrow 0^{+} and the factor in Eq. (S40) becomes 1/Δ​Em​n1/\Delta E_{mn}.

SI.3.1 Long-wavelength limit of the dielectric function

At 𝐪=𝟎\mathbf{q}=\mathbf{0}, one has 𝐆f=𝟎\mathbf{G}_{\mathrm{f}}=\mathbf{0} and 𝐤𝐪=𝐤\mathbf{k}_{\mathbf{q}}=\mathbf{k}. Equation (S39) gives

Mn​m​(𝐤,𝟎)=∑𝐆Zn​𝐆∗​(𝐤)​Zm​𝐆​(𝐤)=δn​m,M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{0})=\sum_{\mathbf{G}}Z^{*}_{n\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{k})Z_{m\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{k})=\delta_{nm}, (S42)

by orthonormality of the Hartree–Fock eigenvectors at fixed 𝐤\mathbf{k}. Since the polarizability in Eq. (S40) contains only occupied–empty terms, n∈occn\in\mathrm{occ} and m∈empm\in\mathrm{emp}, Eq. (S42) implies

ΠHF​(𝟎,0)=0.\Pi_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{0},0)=0. (S43)

For sufficiently small nonzero 𝐪\mathbf{q}, no reciprocal-lattice folding is required for generic 𝐤\mathbf{k}, and the matrix element can be written as an overlap between cell-periodic functions,

Mn​m​(𝐤,𝐪)=⟨un​𝐤|um,𝐤+𝐪⟩.M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})=\left\langle u_{n\mathbf{k}}\middle|u_{m,\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}\right\rangle. (S44)

Expanding the final state in powers of 𝐪\mathbf{q} gives

um,𝐤+𝐪=um​𝐤+∑aqa​∂kaum​𝐤+O⁡(q2),u_{m,\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{q}}=u_{m\mathbf{k}}+\sum_{a}q_{a}\,\partial_{k_{a}}u_{m\mathbf{k}}+O(q^{2}), (S45)

and therefore

Mn​m​(𝐤,𝐪)=δn​m+∑aqa​⟨un​𝐤|∂kaum​𝐤⟩+O⁡(q2).M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})=\delta_{nm}+\sum_{a}q_{a}\left\langle u_{n\mathbf{k}}\middle|\partial_{k_{a}}u_{m\mathbf{k}}\right\rangle+O(q^{2}). (S46)

For an interband occupied–empty transition, n≠mn\neq m, the zeroth-order term vanishes and

Mn​m​(𝐤,𝐪)=O⁡(q),|Mn​m​(𝐤,𝐪)|2=O⁡(q2).M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})=O(q),\qquad\left|M_{nm}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})\right|^{2}=O(q^{2}). (S47)

Because the Wigner-crystal state is insulating, the occupied and empty Hartree–Fock bands are separated by a finite gap,

Δ​Em​n​(𝐤,𝐪)≥ΔHF>0\Delta E_{mn}(\mathbf{k},\mathbf{q})\geq\Delta_{\mathrm{HF}}>0 (S48)

for sufficiently small 𝐪\mathbf{q}. Combining Eqs. (S40) and (S47) gives

ΠHF​(𝐪,0)=O⁡(q2),q→0.\Pi_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0)=O(q^{2}),\qquad q\rightarrow 0. (S49)

The static dielectric function is

εHF​(𝐪,0)=1+v~K​(q)​ΠHF​(𝐪,0).\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0)=1+\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{K}}(q)\Pi_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0). (S50)

For the two-dimensional Keldysh interaction,

v~K​(q)=2​π​e2ε​q​(1+q​ρ0)=2​π​e2ε​q+O⁡(1)(q→0).\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{K}}(q)=\frac{2\pi e^{2}}{\varepsilon q(1+q\rho_{0})}=\frac{2\pi e^{2}}{\varepsilon q}+O(1)\qquad(q\rightarrow 0). (S51)

Therefore

v~K​(q)​ΠHF​(𝐪,0)=O⁡(q),q→0,\widetilde{v}_{\mathrm{K}}(q)\Pi_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0)=O(q),\qquad q\rightarrow 0, (S52)

and the dielectric function is continuous at the origin:

εHF​(𝟎,0)=1,limq→0εHF​(𝐪,0)=1.\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{0},0)=1,\qquad\lim_{q\rightarrow 0}\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(\mathbf{q},0)=1. (S53)

This result is a consequence of the finite insulating gap and the orthogonality of the Hartree–Fock Bloch eigenvectors.

SI.4 Reciprocal-space basis and numerical parameters

The twelve symmetry operations consist of the six rotations C6jC_{6}^{j}, j=0,…,5j=0,\ldots,5, and six mirror operations σj\sigma_{j}. In Miller indices they are represented as

αoperation(m,n)↦(mα,nα)1E(m,n)2C61(−m−n,m)3C62(n,−m−n)4C63(−m,−n)5C64(m+n,−m)6C65(−n,m+n)7σ1(−m−n,n)8σ2(n,m)9σ3(m,−m−n)10σ4(m+n,−n)11σ5(−n,−m)12σ6(−m,m+n)\begin{array}[]{c|c|c}\alpha&\mathrm{operation}&(m,n)\mapsto(m_{\alpha},n_{\alpha})\\ \hline\cr 1&E&(m,n)\\ 2&C_{6}^{1}&(-m-n,m)\\ 3&C_{6}^{2}&(n,-m-n)\\ 4&C_{6}^{3}&(-m,-n)\\ 5&C_{6}^{4}&(m+n,-m)\\ 6&C_{6}^{5}&(-n,m+n)\\ 7&\sigma_{1}&(-m-n,n)\\ 8&\sigma_{2}&(n,m)\\ 9&\sigma_{3}&(m,-m-n)\\ 10&\sigma_{4}&(m+n,-n)\\ 11&\sigma_{5}&(-n,-m)\\ 12&\sigma_{6}&(-m,m+n)\end{array} (S54)

The twelve operations consist of the six rotations C6jC_{6}^{j}, j=0,…,5j=0,\ldots,5, and six mirror operations σj\sigma_{j}. The map in Miller indices is used to generate symmetry images of the k + G expansion while preserving |G| and the closure of the truncated basis. The numerical basis stores the index map 𝐆m​n↦𝐆mα​nα\mathbf{G}_{mn}\mapsto\mathbf{G}_{m_{\alpha}n_{\alpha}} for all retained vectors and all twelve operations. This map is used to generate symmetry images of the 𝐤+𝐆\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G} expansion while preserving |𝐆||\mathbf{G}| and the closure of the truncated basis.

In reduced reciprocal coordinates 𝐤=x​𝐛1+y​𝐛2\mathbf{k}=x\mathbf{b}_{1}+y\mathbf{b}_{2} and the wedge vertices are Γ=(0,0),K=(1/3,1/3),M=(0,1/2)\Gamma=(0,0),K=(1/3,1/3),M=(0,1/2). For a wedge resolution NsideN_{\mathrm{side}}, the mesh is generated row by row. The row index is j=0,…,Nsidej=0,\ldots,N_{\mathrm{side}}, and the point index in that row is t=0,…,2​(Nside−j)t=0,\ldots,2(N_{\mathrm{side}}-j). The corresponding reduced coordinates are

𝐤j​t=t6​Nside​𝐛1+3​j+t6​Nside​𝐛2,\mathbf{k}_{jt}=\frac{t}{6N_{\mathrm{side}}}\mathbf{b}_{1}+\frac{3j+t}{6N_{\mathrm{side}}}\mathbf{b}_{2}, (S55)

and the number of representative wedge points is Nw=∑j=0Nside[2​(Nside−j)+1]=(Nside+1)2N_{w}=\sum_{j=0}^{N_{\mathrm{side}}}\left[2(N_{\mathrm{side}}-j)+1\right]=(N_{\mathrm{side}}+1)^{2}.

Each wedge point represents a set of symmetry-related momenta in the full hexagonal Brillouin zone. Its multiplicity is the number of distinct images generated by the twelve D6D_{6} operations, after identifying momenta equivalent on the periodic Brillouin-zone torus. In the present mesh this gives multiplicity one for Γ\Gamma, two for KK, three for MM, six for non-vertex wedge-boundary points, and twelve for interior wedge points. These multiplicities define the Brillouin-zone weights used in the self-consistent Hartree–Fock sums.

The numerical parameters used in the Hartree–Fock calculations are summarized in Table S1.

SI.5 Full-zone exchange matrix used for the band-structure calculation

The production Hartree–Fock calculation evaluates the exchange matrix by an explicit summation over the full Brillouin-zone mesh. This full mesh is generated from the representative points in the irreducible Γ\Gamma–KK–MM wedge. If 𝐤w\mathbf{k}_{w} is a wedge representative and sws_{w} is its symmetry multiplicity, the distinct full-zone images are

𝐤w​j=Sαj​(w)𝐤w,j=1,…,sw,\mathbf{k}_{wj}=S_{\alpha_{j}(w)}\mathbf{k}_{w},\qquad j=1,\ldots,s_{w}, (S56)

where SαS_{\alpha} denotes one of the twelve D6D_{6} operations and αj​(w)\alpha_{j}(w) is the compact list of operations that generate distinct images of 𝐤w\mathbf{k}_{w} on the periodic Brillouin-zone torus. The full-zone mesh size is therefore

Nfull=∑wsw,N_{\mathrm{full}}=\sum_{w}s_{w}, (S57)

and the weights satisfy ∑ℓ=1Nfullwℓ=1\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_{\mathrm{full}}}w_{\ell}=1. For a uniform full-zone mesh, wℓ=1/Nfullw_{\ell}=1/N_{\mathrm{full}}.

The eigenvectors on the full zone are reconstructed from the wedge eigenvectors using the reciprocal-vector symmetry map. If 𝐤ℓ=Sα​𝐤w\mathbf{k}_{\ell}=S_{\alpha}\mathbf{k}_{w}, then

Zν​𝐆full​(𝐤ℓ)=Zν,Sα−1​𝐆wedge​(𝐤w).Z^{\mathrm{full}}_{\nu\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{k}_{\ell})=Z^{\mathrm{wedge}}_{\nu,S_{\alpha}^{-1}\mathbf{G}}(\mathbf{k}_{w}). (S58)

In the code this operation is implemented by the integer Miller-index map 𝐆m​n↦Sα​𝐆m​n\mathbf{G}_{mn}\mapsto S_{\alpha}\mathbf{G}_{mn}, stored as an index map over the retained GG-star basis.

For a target wedge momentum 𝐤\mathbf{k}, the positive exchange matrix is then computed as

X𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤)\displaystyle X_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}) =1AW∑ℓ=1Nfullwℓ∑𝐆1Zν​𝐆1full(𝐤ℓ)Zν,𝐆1−𝐆+𝐆′full∗(𝐤ℓ)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{A_{W}}\sum_{\ell=1}^{N_{\mathrm{full}}}w_{\ell}\sum_{\mathbf{G}_{1}}Z^{\mathrm{full}}_{\nu\mathbf{G}_{1}}(\mathbf{k}_{\ell})Z^{\mathrm{full}*}_{\nu,\mathbf{G}_{1}-\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}_{\ell})
×v~​[(𝐤+𝐆)−(𝐤ℓ+𝐆1)].\displaystyle\quad\times\widetilde{v}\!\left[(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})-(\mathbf{k}_{\ell}+\mathbf{G}_{1})\right]. (S59)

The shifted index appearing in Eq. (S59) follows from the selection rule in Eq. (S24). The Hartree–Fock matrix used in the diagonalization is therefore

h𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤)=T𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤)+V𝐆𝐆′H−X𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤).h_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})=T_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k})+V^{H}_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}-X_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}). (S60)

Equivalently, one may avoid forming the explicit full-zone list by writing the same exchange sum as a wedge sum over representatives and their distinct symmetry images,

X𝐆𝐆′​(𝐤)\displaystyle X_{\mathbf{G}\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(\mathbf{k}) =1AW∑w∑j=1swww​j∑𝐆1Zν​𝐆1full(Sαj​(w)𝐤w)Zν,𝐆1−𝐆+𝐆′full∗(Sαj​(w)𝐤w)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{A_{W}}\sum_{w}\sum_{j=1}^{s_{w}}w_{wj}\sum_{\mathbf{G}_{1}}Z^{\mathrm{full}}_{\nu\mathbf{G}_{1}}(S_{\alpha_{j}(w)}\mathbf{k}_{w})Z^{\mathrm{full}*}_{\nu,\mathbf{G}_{1}-\mathbf{G}+\mathbf{G}^{\prime}}(S_{\alpha_{j}(w)}\mathbf{k}_{w})
×v~​[(𝐤+𝐆)−(Sαj​(w)​𝐤w+𝐆1)].\displaystyle\quad\times\widetilde{v}\!\left[(\mathbf{k}+\mathbf{G})-(S_{\alpha_{j}(w)}\mathbf{k}_{w}+\mathbf{G}_{1})\right]. (S61)

This form is algebraically equivalent to Eq. (S59); the production results reported here use the explicit full-BZ form, which is less compact but avoids additional bookkeeping inside the exchange summation.

SI.6 Interpretation of the maximum of the static dielectric function

The maximum of εHF​(q,0)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0) provides additional information about the momentum-transfer dependence of screening in the Wigner-crystal state. We denote by qmaxq_{\max} the momentum at which εHF​(q,0)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0) reaches its maximum. This is the momentum transfer for which the additional electronic screening produced by the resident Wigner crystal is strongest.

The existence of a maximum at finite qq follows from the insulating and crystalline character of the Hartree–Fock solution. In the long-wavelength limit, the Wigner crystal does not provide a metallic intraband response. Accordingly, the density response is suppressed and εHF​(q,0)→1\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0)\rightarrow 1 as q→0q\rightarrow 0. At large qq, the Keldysh interaction is weaker and the density-matrix form factors entering the Hartree–Fock polarizability become less effective. The strongest static screening therefore occurs at an intermediate momentum, where the interaction strength, the interband density matrix elements, and the Hartree–Fock excitation energies combine to produce the largest screening correction.

For carrier–carrier scattering, momentum transfers close to qmaxq_{\max} are the ones most strongly renormalized by the electronic response of the Wigner crystal. In this sense, qmaxq_{\max} identifies the most efficient momentum-transfer channel for static screening in the crystalline state. This does not make qmaxq_{\max} a thermodynamic order parameter; rather, it is a finite-qq response scale associated with the self-consistent crystalline Hartree–Fock state.

The shift of qmaxq_{\max} toward smaller absolute momenta with increasing rsr_{s} is consistent with the decrease of the reciprocal-lattice scale as the Wigner-crystal lattice constant increases. For a triangular Wigner crystal, the magnitude of the first reciprocal-lattice vector is

G1=4​π3​aL,G_{1}=\frac{4\pi}{\sqrt{3}a_{L}}, (S62)

where aLa_{L} is the Wigner-crystal lattice constant. Since aLa_{L} increases with rsr_{s}, the characteristic reciprocal-lattice scale decreases. The finite-qq features in εHF​(q,0)\varepsilon_{\mathrm{HF}}(q,0) are therefore naturally displaced toward smaller absolute momenta in the dilute regime.
